notes: Crop knowledge base. Thresholds and stage vulnerabilities come from the evidence table compiled 2026-11-19 (land-grant extension, USDA, Canola Council); source IDs (S01...) map to 'references'. Levels describe WEATHER INTENSITY for the crop; the engine then adjusts for crop exposure (share of the crop in vulnerable phases) and forecast lead time. All values are configurable.

freeze.vulnerable: Most vulnerable before physiological maturity (black layer, R6), especially during grain fill (R4-R5); seedlings are partly protected until about V5-V6 because the growing point is below ground.
freeze.short_term: Leaf injury shows within 1-3 days. Several hours at or below 32 F, or a short time at 28 F, can kill immature plants; young corn at 28-32 F usually suffers leaf damage only.
freeze.medium_term: A killing freeze before black layer ends grain fill early; published estimates are roughly 40-55% yield loss at R4-R5 and about 12% at half milkline, with no loss at black layer. Frost-killed corn dries down more slowly.
freeze.implications: Possible lower yield and test weight, light kernels, slower field drydown and later harvest, and weaker stalks. Corn at black layer is not affected.
monitor: Share of fields not yet at black layer (R6)
Low-lying field areas, which can run several degrees colder than nearby stations
Regrowth from the whorl 3-5 days after a spring frost
Stalk integrity and drydown in frost-killed fields

heat.vulnerable: Pollination (VT-R1) and the two weeks before and after silking.
heat.short_term: Temperatures in the mid-90s F and above, especially with low humidity, can dry exposed silks and reduce pollen viability; above 100 F pollen can be killed.
heat.medium_term: About four or more hot days during pollination can reduce kernel set (roughly 1% per day in one study with adequate moisture), with larger losses when soils are dry.
heat.implications: Fewer kernels per ear and lower yield potential; effects are much larger when heat coincides with drought.
monitor: Share of fields shedding pollen or silking
Consecutive days at or above 95 F
Soil moisture and afternoon leaf rolling

drought.vulnerable: Highest sensitivity from about two weeks before silking through early grain fill (V12-R2).
drought.short_term: Leaf rolling and wilting; estimated yield losses of roughly 3-9% per day of stress around pollination and 2-5% per day in late vegetative stages.
drought.medium_term: Fewer kernels per ear (before/at silking) or lighter kernels (grain fill); prolonged drought can force early maturity.
drought.implications: Lower yield potential and test weight.
monitor: Drought Monitor category changes week to week
Observed rainfall over the last 2-4 weeks

heavy_rain.vulnerable: Young corn before V6, when the growing point is at or below the soil surface; ears of dented corn if submerged.
heavy_rain.short_term: Ponded seedlings generally survive about 4 days when air is below about 77 F but may not survive 24 hours when warmer; soil oxygen is depleted within about 48 hours.
heavy_rain.medium_term: Stand loss, nitrogen loss and disease can reduce yield (5-32% in published flooding studies); submerged mature ears can develop ear rot.
heavy_rain.implications: Replant decisions in spring, delayed field operations, possible grain quality issues.
monitor: Hours of standing water in low spots
Air temperature while fields are ponded
New leaf growth 3-5 days after water recedes

harvest_rain.vulnerable: Mature corn still standing in the field.
harvest_rain.short_term: Rain and cool, cloudy days can stop field drydown and delay combining.
harvest_rain.medium_term: Long delays raise the risk of stalk lodging, ear drop and harvest losses and increase drying costs.
harvest_rain.implications: Slower harvest progress and higher grain moisture at harvest.
monitor: Harvest progress versus the 5-year average (USDA NASS)

severe_storm.vulnerable: Late vegetative stages through pollination; before about V6 the growing point is protected and leaf loss rarely affects yield.
severe_storm.short_term: Hail can defoliate and bruise stalks; wind can snap stalks (greensnap) during rapid elongation (about V5-V8 and V12 to tassel) or root-lodge plants.
severe_storm.medium_term: Insurance loss tables estimate yield loss at 100% defoliation of about 16-51% in mid-vegetative stages and near-total loss at tasseling; early root lodging usually recovers.
severe_storm.implications: Yield and quality losses, slower harvest if lodged, possible disease entry through wounds.
monitor: Defoliation and stand counts 7-10 days after a storm
Crop stage at the time of the storm

high_wind.vulnerable: Rapid stalk elongation (V12 to tassel) for greensnap; mature corn with weakened stalks for lodging.
high_wind.short_term: Stalk breakage or lodging; frost- or disease-weakened mature stalks are more prone to lodging and ear drop.
high_wind.medium_term: Yield loss roughly proportional to snapped plants (about 0.5-1% per 1% of plants snapped); lodged fields harvest more slowly.
high_wind.implications: Harvest losses and slower combining in lodged fields.
monitor: Stalk quality before strong wind events

winter_storm.vulnerable: Corn still standing in the field after maturity.
winter_storm.short_term: Snow and ice halt harvest and can push down weakened stalks.
winter_storm.medium_term: Prolonged delays increase field losses (lodging, ear drop) and drying costs.
winter_storm.implications: Slower harvest completion and potential grain losses.
monitor: Lodging in standing fields after the storm

outlook_wet.vulnerable: Unharvested mature corn (harvest delays) or recently planted fields.
outlook_wet.short_term: Outlook only: a wetter-than-normal signal 8-14 days out, not a rainfall forecast.
outlook_wet.medium_term: If realized, wetter weeks could slow remaining field work.
monitor: NWS 7-day rainfall forecasts as the period approaches

freeze.vulnerable: Before beginning maturity (R7), especially during pod development and seed fill (R3-R6); emerged seedlings are more exposed than corn because the growing point is above ground.
freeze.short_term: Below 32 F leaves can be damaged; below 30 F for an extended period stems, pods and seeds can be injured; 28 F is considered a killing freeze.
freeze.medium_term: A killing freeze at R5 can cut yield by up to about half and by roughly 10% at R6; fields with mature-color pods (R7) are minimally affected.
freeze.implications: Lower yield, green or shriveled seed (a grading damage factor), slower drying and more shatter at harvest.
monitor: Share of fields before R7 (USDA 'dropping leaves')
Green seed and moisture readings at harvest

heat.short_term: Several consecutive days above about 85-90 F slow photosynthesis and can cause flower and pod abortion, especially with dry soils.
heat.medium_term: Fewer pods and smaller seed; heat can hasten maturity.
heat.implications: Lower yield potential; largest when heat and drought coincide. Evidence for soybean heat thresholds is moderate.
monitor: Consecutive days at or above 90-95 F during flowering and pod set
Pod counts after the heat event

drought.short_term: Peak water use (about 0.3 in per day at R2-R3) means dry spells quickly cause stress.
drought.medium_term: Drought at R3-R4 reduces pods and seeds per acre; at R5-R6 it reduces seed size and hastens maturity; pod number can fall by up to about 20%.

heavy_rain.vulnerable: Emerged seedlings and early vegetative plants; waterlogging at R2 costs more than in vegetative stages.
heavy_rain.short_term: Survival is generally good under 48 hours of flooding and up to about 7 days when air is below 80 F; saturated soils approach zero oxygen in 24-48 hours.
heavy_rain.medium_term: Short waterlogging (2-3 days) at V2-V4 has reduced yields from 0 to 50% in studies; nodulation suffers after 7-10 days of saturation.
heavy_rain.implications: Stand loss, replant decisions, yellowing and slower growth.
monitor: Stand counts 3-5 days after water recedes

harvest_rain.short_term: Rain delays harvest; repeated wetting and drying increases shatter and lowers seed germination.
harvest_rain.medium_term: Prolonged warm, humid weather favors seed decay fungi and sprouting in the pod.
harvest_rain.implications: Harvest losses and lower seed quality and grade.
monitor: Shatter and pod splitting in standing fields

severe_storm.vulnerable: Reproductive stages, especially R4-R5; leaf loss in vegetative stages has little yield effect.
severe_storm.short_term: Hail defoliation and broken stems and pods; wind can shatter pods of mature beans.
severe_storm.medium_term: Insurance tables estimate yield loss at 100% defoliation of about 33% at R3 and 75-84% at R5; reproductive stand loss costs about 1% yield per 1% of stand.
monitor: Defoliation and stand counts after storms
Crop stage at the time of the storm

high_wind.short_term: Pod shatter and lodging in standing mature fields.
high_wind.medium_term: Harvest losses rise the longer mature beans stand in the field.

winter_storm.vulnerable: Soybeans still standing in the field.
winter_storm.short_term: Snow halts harvest and can flatten plants.
winter_storm.medium_term: Delays increase shatter and pod losses.

outlook_wet.vulnerable: Unharvested mature soybeans or recently planted fields.
outlook_wet.short_term: Outlook only: a wetter-than-normal signal 8-14 days out, not a rainfall forecast.
outlook_wet.medium_term: If realized, wetter weeks could slow remaining field work and affect seed quality.

canola.label: Canola
canola.calendar_source: S01 (OK); S40 and S48 agronomic windows (ND, MN, SD, KS; approximate)

freeze.vulnerable: Spring canola: seedlings (exposed growing point), flowering and especially seed fill before seed moisture falls below about 20%. Winter canola: flowering and pod set in spring.
freeze.short_term: Hardened spring-canola seedlings tolerate about 24 F, unhardened plants can die at about 25-27 F, and frost at flowering aborts only open flowers. Winter canola exposed to the mid-20s F at flowering can show aborted flowers, bent racemes and split stems.
freeze.medium_term: Frost after flowering can cause large yield and grade losses; below about 23 F is generally lethal to high-moisture seed, and frosts near 32 F can leave green seed.
freeze.implications: Green seed (main grade loss), shriveled seed, delayed maturity, lodging from split stems.
monitor: Plant survival 4-10 days after frost (green growing point)
Seed color change and seed moisture before a freeze
Duration of the frost (an all-night light frost can be severe)

extreme_cold.vulnerable: Overwintering winter-canola rosettes, especially small plants (fewer than 3 true leaves), plants with an elevated crown, and plants that lost hardiness during warm spells.
extreme_cold.short_term: Winter survival is linked to several days with daily mean temperatures between about 5 and 14 F, many freeze-thaw cycles and strong wind chill; no single lethal air temperature is established. Snow cover is not measured by this platform.
extreme_cold.medium_term: Winterkill reduces stands; leaf loss over winter is acceptable if the crown survives; snow cover insulates plants.
extreme_cold.implications: Stand loss and possible replant or abandonment decisions in spring.
monitor: Fall plant size (6-8 true leaves with the crown near the soil surface is optimal)
Crown survival once average temperatures rise above about 40 F

heat.vulnerable: Bolting through the end of flowering.
heat.short_term: Above about 85-86 F, open flowers may fail to pollinate.
heat.medium_term: Reduced seed yield; heat during seed formation lowers oil content.
heat.implications: Yield and oil-content losses, larger with drought.
monitor: Days at or above 86 F during flowering

drought.vulnerable: Flowering and pod/seed fill; for winter canola also fall establishment (plants need adequate size before winter).
drought.short_term: Canola is less drought tolerant than small grains; moisture stress at flowering reduces pod set.
drought.medium_term: Lower yield; small fall plants enter winter with higher winterkill risk.

heavy_rain.vulnerable: All growth stages; flowering is most affected.
heavy_rain.short_term: Yield reduction is common after only 3 consecutive days of waterlogging.
heavy_rain.medium_term: Fewer pods per branch and seeds per pod, worse with high temperatures.
heavy_rain.implications: Yield losses in poorly drained fields.

harvest_rain.vulnerable: Mature or swathed canola awaiting harvest.
harvest_rain.short_term: Rain on mature canola weakens pods and increases shatter.
harvest_rain.medium_term: Delayed straight-cutting averaged about 15% yield loss in prairie trials.

severe_storm.vulnerable: Pod fill and maturity; early-season hail is usually recovered.
severe_storm.short_term: Hail and wind can shatter mature pods; losses above 50% are possible at harvest.
severe_storm.medium_term: Replacement branching can compensate for early damage but not for losses at maturity.
severe_storm.implications: Yield losses, especially close to harvest.
monitor: Stand and pod damage after storms
Crop stage at the time of the storm

high_wind.short_term: Strong winds can shatter mature pods and move swaths.

freeze.vulnerable: Bud and flowering stages are the most frost-sensitive; emerging seedlings tolerate about 26 F; risk becomes minimal at physiological maturity (R9).
freeze.short_term: About 30 F or below injures open florets; 25 F at bud often damages the stalk below the bud; a general killing freeze is about 24 F for 2 hours.
freeze.medium_term: Frost before full maturity lowers yield, oil content and test weight; 10-14 days after petal drying, plants tolerate about 25 F with only minor damage.
freeze.implications: Yield, oil and test-weight losses in immature fields; mature (R9) fields are minimally affected.
monitor: Share of fields before R9 (back of head yellow, bracts brown)
Hours at or below 28 F and 24 F
Seed fill and test weight in frosted fields

heat.short_term: High temperatures during seed formation change the oil profile; hot, dry conditions favor charcoal rot.
heat.medium_term: No numeric yield threshold was found in extension sources, so this is treated as a monitoring signal only.
monitor: Signs of charcoal rot in hot, dry fields

drought.vulnerable: Bud through flowering (R2-R5.9) is the most water-sensitive period.
drought.short_term: Daily water use exceeds about 0.27 in from head emergence to full head.
drought.medium_term: Excessive soil-water depletion during R2-R5.9 has cut yields by about 50% in research cited by NDSU.
drought.implications: Yield losses; emergence to early bud is least sensitive.
monitor: Crop stage relative to bud and flowering

heavy_rain.vulnerable: All growth stages in poorly drained fields.
heavy_rain.short_term: Plants flooded for more than about three days may not recover.
heavy_rain.implications: Replant decisions early in the season; yield loss later.

harvest_rain.short_term: Rain delays harvest and slows drydown; natural-air drying times double near 27 F.
harvest_rain.medium_term: Delays increase blackbird damage, lodging and head losses.
harvest_rain.implications: Harvest losses and higher drying costs.
monitor: Seed moisture (harvest at up to about 25%)

severe_storm.short_term: Hail stand loss at R4-R6 reduces yield roughly one-for-one (10% stand loss is about 10% yield loss); stalk breakage risk is greatest at maturity.
severe_storm.medium_term: Defoliation of 30% costs about 3-10% yield depending on stage.
severe_storm.implications: Yield losses and harvest difficulty in broken or lodged fields.
monitor: Stand and head damage after storms

high_wind.vulnerable: Mature sunflowers, especially under drought stress or heavy stem weevil infestation.
high_wind.short_term: Stalk breakage and lodging risk is greatest at maturity.

winter_storm.vulnerable: Sunflowers still standing in the field.
winter_storm.short_term: Snow halts harvest of remaining fields.
winter_storm.medium_term: Standing heads are exposed to lodging and bird damage while harvest is delayed.
winter_storm.implications: Harvest losses for the remaining acreage.

outlook_wet.short_term: Outlook only: a wetter-than-normal signal 8-14 days out, not a rainfall forecast.
outlook_wet.medium_term: If realized, wetter weeks could slow the remaining harvest.

sugarcane.label: Sugarcane
sugarcane.calendar_source: S01 (LA harvest end extended to Jan 10 to reflect recent ~4-month milling seasons noted by LSU AgCenter, S70)

freeze.vulnerable: Standing (unharvested) cane during the harvest season; stubble and ratoons are mostly protected below ground unless the soil freezes.
freeze.short_term: LSU AgCenter freeze categories: 32 to 25 F kills terminal buds and leaves but usually not the stalk; 25 to 22 F also kills lateral buds and can damage stalk tissue; below 22 F kills all above-ground parts.
freeze.medium_term: After damaging freezes, bacteria can convert sucrose to dextran. In LSU trials quality changed little for 2 weeks, was harmed by about 3 weeks and was unacceptable for processing by about 30 days; warm weather after a freeze speeds deterioration. In Florida trials, freezes of 24.8 F or colder hastened juice deterioration.
freeze.implications: Growers and mills may reprioritize harvest toward damaged and less cold-tolerant varieties; sugar recovery and juice quality can decline. A light freeze (32-25 F) mainly affects leaves and terminal buds.
monitor: Hours at or below 25 F and 22 F in each parish or county
Field-by-field damage once the full extent shows (up to about a week)
Temperatures after the freeze (warm weather speeds deterioration)
Variety cold tolerance and remaining standing acreage

heavy_rain.vulnerable: Harvest operations in standing cane; established cane tolerates temporary flooding.
heavy_rain.short_term: Saturated fields slow cutting and hauling.
heavy_rain.medium_term: Established cane showed no yield or sugar effect from flooding of up to 2 weeks in a USDA-ARS study, but persistently shallow water tables reduced yields.
heavy_rain.implications: Harvest delays rather than direct crop loss in most cases.

harvest_rain.vulnerable: Standing cane during the harvest and milling season.
harvest_rain.short_term: Wet fields delay cutting and hauling.
harvest_rain.medium_term: Delays push harvest into colder weeks; growers and mills aim to finish most harvest before January because late seasons raise freeze exposure.
harvest_rain.implications: Harvest scheduling and freeze exposure of the remaining crop.
monitor: Freeze outlook for the remaining harvest window

high_wind.vulnerable: Tall cane late in the growing season.
high_wind.short_term: Strong winds can lodge cane; lodged cane usually partly re-erects within about a week.
high_wind.medium_term: The growth pause costs some tonnage, and lodged cane is more vulnerable to freeze damage.

severe_storm.medium_term: Lodged cane partly re-erects within about a week; some tonnage loss.

drought.short_term: Reported for context; no crop-specific drought threshold was verified for sugarcane.

outlook_cold.vulnerable: Standing cane during the harvest season.
outlook_cold.short_term: Outlook only: a colder-than-normal signal 8-14 days out raises the chance of freezes while cane is still standing; it is not a freeze forecast.
outlook_cold.medium_term: If freezes follow, harvest priorities may shift toward less cold-tolerant varieties.
monitor: NWS 7-day lows as the period approaches
